title: Surfing App
subtitle: A mobile telemetry and progression system designed to help surfers track wave mechanics before, during, and after a session.

thumbnail.placeholderHTML: Surfing App

hero.placeholderHTML: [ Surfing App Hero Visual ]

solution.content:
How can wave tracking survive the friction of an active surf session?

Surfing depends heavily on environmental intuition. Most digital surf tools help users prepare before entering the water, but the moment the session begins, the feedback loop breaks.

This project explores a mobile ecosystem designed around that gap. It connects predictive ocean data, active session tracking, personal progression, and local surf support into one continuous experience.

The challenge was not simply to design another sports-tracking app. It was to design an interface that could survive glare, water, motion, interrupted attention, and the physical rhythm of surfing without breaking the user’s state of flow.

Hero visual slot: phone mockup, wave map, telemetry overlay, or animated session screen

Behavioral Research

Understanding how surfers interact with digital tools before, during, and after a session.

Environmental Prototyping

Testing how glare, water, motion, and touch inaccuracy affect interface decisions.

Session-Based Continuity

Designing a system that preserves context across interrupted, fragmented interactions.

An interruption-tolerant tracking system built for the water.

The Surfing App is a conceptual mobile platform that tracks wave mechanics and physical performance through a simplified, high-contrast interface.

The product is structured around session-based continuity. Instead of treating every screen as a separate interaction, the app preserves the active session state until the user manually ends it.

This allows the surfer to interact in short bursts without losing context. The system also extends beyond active tracking through progression journaling, embedded tutorials, and localized equipment rentals.

Session-Based Continuity

The app preserves active session data without requiring manual saves. This matters because surfers interact with devices in short, interrupted moments and cannot afford to restart tracking logic mid-session.

Glanceable Telemetry

The interface prioritizes one key metric at a time. It avoids dense dashboards because bright sunlight, movement, and water droplets make complex UI layouts harder to read.

Progression Journaling and Embedded Classes

Users can log named tricks, review personal bests, and access video tutorials. The app becomes a learning system, not just a tracking surface.

Localized Equipment Marketplace

The app connects users to local surf shops for rentals and gear access. This reduces friction for tourists who often face hidden charges or fragmented local information.

Solution visual slot: final app screens, onboarding flow, active tracking UI, progression journal, rental module

flows.content:
The experience is built around two high-friction moments: entering the water and returning from it.

The core flows were designed to reduce interaction during the session and move deeper reflection to the moment after the surfer returns to land.

Flow 1: Session Setup

Trigger: The user initiates a new surf session on the beach.

Action: The user defines location and targets with a simple setup interaction.

System response: The app locks the screen for water use and begins background telemetry.

Value: It removes pre-entry friction and prevents accidental touches in the water.

Flow 2: Skill Progression Logging

Trigger: The user completes a session and returns to land.

Action: The user reviews telemetry and logs named tricks.

System response: The app connects trick timestamps with localized wave-pattern data.

Value: It builds a personal progression journal and contributes to long-term wave behavior mapping.

Flow 3: Equipment and Learning Support

Trigger: A tourist or beginner needs gear, lessons, or skill guidance.

Action: The user browses trusted rental options or embedded learning content.

System response: The app surfaces localized support without relying on informal networks.

Value: It reduces the cost and trust barrier around surf coaching and rentals.

Flow visual slot: journey map, app flow diagram, session loop animation, or wireflow

research.content:
Users checked their phones before entering the water, then abandoned the interface completely.

To understand the friction points of aquatic tech use, the research combined rapid early validation with deeper behavioral observation.

Synthetic Users were used to generate early interview patterns and pressure-test assumptions. These were followed by contextual inquiry and diary-style observation to understand how surfers actually behave before, during, and after sessions.

Method: Contextual Inquiry

Used to understand the physical and environmental conditions around surf preparation, device use, and session entry.

Method: Diary Studies

Used to observe patterns across sessions rather than relying only on one-time recall.

Method: Synthetic User AI Testing

Used for rapid early validation and to identify possible friction points before moving into grounded research.

Method: Quantitative Behavioral Parsing

Used to make sense of repeated behavioral patterns and translate them into product decisions.

Research visual slot: observation notes, journey mapping, research synthesis clusters, or insight cards

The Pre-Entry Wall

Users leave devices behind because current interfaces are not usable when wet. The design implication was clear: the app needed an aquatic lock state and passive tracking capabilities.

The Coaching Cost Barrier

Tourists and beginners often navigate steep costs, hidden charges, and unreliable local networks. This shaped the decision to include tutorials and trusted rental access.

The Voice UI Trap

Voice interaction seemed relevant at first, but the surfing environment made it unreliable. The final interface avoids voice input and depends on visual clarity instead.

formFactors.content:
The project shifted from feature density to environmental restraint.

Early exploration focused on how much information the app should expose during a session. The strongest direction was not the one with the most features, but the one that asked the least from the user while they were physically engaged with the water.

Audio-First Feedback

What it was: A waterproof earbud-based flow that delivered wave stats through an AI voice layer.

Why it seemed promising: It bypassed the screen visibility problem completely.

Why it changed: Ocean acoustics made voice input and feedback unreliable. Repeating commands would break concentration and increase frustration.

High-Density Dashboard

What it was: A data-heavy screen showing wind, swell, tide, and performance metrics together.

Why it seemed promising: It gave the user more control over environmental variables.

Why it changed: It caused too much cognitive load during the session and became harder to read in glare and motion.

Simplified Visual Telemetry

Where the direction landed: The final direction prioritizes one metric at a time through a high-contrast interface, while the system architecture remembers the larger session context in the background.

Exploration visual slot: rejected voice UI concept, dense dashboard concept, simplified telemetry comparison

prototyping.content:
Testing revealed that visibility was not only about contrast. It was about motion, context, and device behavior.

Due to the eight-week timeline, the project moved quickly from ideation into mid-fidelity prototyping. Crazy Eights was used for rapid concept generation, Relume supported early information architecture, and Figma was used to build testable greyscale prototypes.

The goal was not to perfect visual design early. It was to expose the interaction model to physical and behavioral stress as quickly as possible.

Prototype visual slot: Figma mid-fidelity screens, greyscale flow, or before-after interface iterations

Testing Insight 1: High contrast can still create discomfort

Senior stakeholders noted that the initial high-contrast palette could induce motion discomfort or visual vibration in moving water. The color system was recalibrated to reduce harshness while retaining legibility.

Testing Insight 2: Hardware variation changes the interaction model

One user attempted to interact with the prototype on a folded Samsung flip phone. This revealed that aquatic hardware constraints go beyond waterproofing. Form factor, viewport, and touch target behavior need to be treated as future design requirements.

Testing Insight 3: Scope had to protect the core interaction

The first version remained locked to a standard viewport so the session logic could be resolved clearly before expanding into responsive edge cases.

decisions.content:
The final design was shaped by environmental realities, not interface trends.

Decision 1: Preserve the session until the user ends it

Problem: Users frequently lose context when an app auto-locks, reloads, or resets during physical activity.

Options considered: Standard app state management versus persistent background session logic.

Final decision: The active state remains continuous until manually stopped.

Rationale: This mirrors the mental model of surfing as one continuous physical session.

Tradeoff: It requires more complex backend state logic.

Decision 2: Remove AI voice interaction

Problem: Users cannot easily look at screens while paddling or moving through water.

Options considered: Voice agents versus high-contrast visual feedback.

Final decision: Voice interaction was removed entirely.

Rationale: Muffled acoustics and ocean noise made voice models too unreliable for this context.

Tradeoff: The user still needs occasional visual attention, but the system avoids misinterpreted commands.

Decision 3: Include the market ecosystem lightly

Problem: Tourists face hidden charges when seeking coaching or renting surf equipment.

Options considered: A pure telemetry app versus an integrated support ecosystem.

Final decision: The app includes a lightweight rental and embedded video class module.

Rationale: It responds to a real pain point while giving the product a stronger retention loop.

Tradeoff: It increases the information architecture scope.

Design decision visual slot: system logic diagram, voice UI rejection diagram, or feature tradeoff matrix

hardware.content:
Designing for an interface that is wet, glaring, and moving.

The interface had to respond to a hostile environment. The screen was not treated as a stable surface. It was treated as something affected by water, glare, inaccurate touch, interruptions, and body movement.

Eight-Week Time Constraint

The timeline limited the ability to design a fully responsive ecosystem from day one. The first version stayed locked to a single viewport so the core session logic could be resolved well.

High Glare

Sunlight makes subtle UI elements disappear. The interface removed soft grayscale dependence and moved toward stronger contrast and clearer hierarchy.

Touch Inaccuracy

Wet fingers and screens increase mis-taps. Standard tap targets were replaced by larger, simpler interaction zones where possible.

Constraint visual slot: glare test, wet-screen touch diagram, hardware stress states, or responsive notes

reflection.content:
Moving from screen-led to context-led design.

Scoping against trends

This project reinforced the importance of ignoring industry trends when the context demands it. Voice AI was a strong trend during the project, but the ocean made it unreliable. The best technology was not the most current one. It was the one that worked in the user’s environment.

Designing for hostile environments

The surfing context forced the interface to become more disciplined. Decorative UI had to be stripped away because every pixel needed to support visibility, orientation, or action.

Systems thinking in state management

The strongest learning was that good UX is not only about the screen in front of the user. It is also about how the system remembers what the user was doing. Session-based continuity became the anchor of the entire product.

This project clarified a larger design belief: digital architecture should adapt to human behavior, instead of forcing people to adapt to the screen.
